title: Estimating synergy soberly: why most deals fall short
subtitle: The number on the slide, the premium paid, and five ways to cut the optimism out
openingQuestion: The buyer pays 30% above the market price. What has to be true for the deal to create value?
openingOptions: Combined revenue has to exceed the sum of the two sides
Discounted synergy has to exceed the premium paid
Earnings per share must rise in the very first year
The target must carry the higher profit margin
explanation: The premium over the market price goes straight to the seller's shareholders, so the buyer has only the synergy left to make it back. If the present value of the synergy is smaller than the premium already paid, value moves from the buyer's shareholders to the seller's - the deal still closes, the company is still bigger, and the buyer's shareholders are poorer. Higher combined revenue is automatic when you add two companies together and says nothing about value. A rise in earnings per share settles nothing either, because it depends on whether you paid in cash or in stock rather than on whether the deal was worth doing.

diagram.label: Compare with the present value of the synergy
Only synergy larger than the premium creates value

realWorldExample.description: The cost savings from closing overlapping branches usually land close to the plan, because they turn on an internal decision. The cross-selling of products into each other's customer bases tends to fall short, because it turns on whether the customers stay and whether they buy more - two things nobody inside the deal controls.

quiz.question: How do cost synergy and revenue synergy differ in how certain they are?
options: Cost synergy is the more reliable of the two
Revenue synergy is more reliable, being easier to size
The two carry equal certainty in practice
It depends on the sector and its kind of overlap
quiz.explanation: Cost synergy - removing duplicated headcount, closing overlapping branches, consolidating IT systems - is internal and therefore manageable. Revenue synergy - cross-selling and upselling into each other's customer base - depends on customer behaviour and is far harder to predict. Revenue synergy is not easier to size, the two are plainly not equally certain, and the industry changes the size of the prize rather than which type is more dependable.

quiz.question: What is an acquisition premium normally justified by?
options: The book value of the target company
The present value of the expected synergies
The ego and emotion of the buyer's management
Pressure to close from the advising bank
quiz.explanation: The acquisition premium - typically 20-40% over the market price - has to be justified by synergy. If PV(synergy) exceeds the premium paid, the deal creates value; if it does not, the M&A destroys value, which is why so large a share of deals disappoint. Book value is a historical accounting figure with no bearing on it, and ego or banker pressure explain why premiums get paid, not why they are defensible.

quiz.question: Why does synergy tend to get overestimated?
options: Bankers and management are paid to make the deal happen
It is hard to compute exactly, so everyone rounds upward
Integration always takes longer than anybody planned for
All three of the reasons above contribute together
quiz.explanation: Bankers earn advisory fees and management want a larger empire, so both sides have an incentive to overstate synergy. On top of that, integration is genuinely harder than the model assumes: culture clash, IT systems to merge, customers who may leave while it is happening. Each of the first three answers is real on its own; the mistake is treating any one of them as the whole explanation.

quiz.question: What is run-rate synergy?
options: The synergy actually achieved in the first year
Revenue synergy that comes from cross-selling
Synergy arising from operations rather than from sales
The annualised synergy level once fully implemented
quiz.explanation: Run-rate synergy is the annual synergy once the programme is fully implemented. Example: closing 10 offices saves 100bn a year, but it takes 18 months to close them all, so the run rate is 100bn while year one delivers only 50bn. That gap between the run rate and the first year is exactly what the first option confuses, and the source of the saving is a separate question from when it arrives.

quiz.question: In synergy analysis, what is 'dis-synergy'?
options: Negative synergy - value destroyed after the merger
Synergy that is hard to put a specific number on
Synergy that takes several years to be achieved
Synergy that is merely delayed rather than lost
quiz.explanation: Dis-synergy is negative synergy. Buying a luxury brand and diluting its exclusive image cuts revenue; a culture clash that makes key talent leave destroys value the same way. It has to be netted off the synergy estimate. Being hard to measure, arriving late, or being delayed are all timing and precision problems - dis-synergy is a loss that never comes back.

keyTakeaways: The premium goes to the seller's shareholders immediately; the buyer has only synergy left to make it back
Cost savings are more dependable than revenue growth, because they sit in the buyer's own hands
Whoever builds the number has an incentive for the deal to happen, so the first figure is almost always optimistic
One-off integration costs usually equal one to two years of synergy and are routinely left out of the model

practicePrompt.question: The banker puts synergy at 100bn a year. You haircut it to 60%, and the one-off integration cost equals one year of the haircut synergy. What is left in year one?
options: 0bn: 60 of synergy less 60 of integration cost
60bn: integration cost falls into the later years
40bn: 100bn less 60bn of integration cost
100bn: integration cost does not belong here
practicePrompt.explanation: Haircutting 100bn to 60% gives 60bn, and a one-off integration cost equal to one year of the haircut synergy is also 60bn - so year one comes to nothing. That is why a deal that looks handsome on the slide can still contribute nothing in its first year, and why synergy has to be viewed year by year rather than only at the full run rate. The 40bn answer makes the mistake of deducting the cost from the figure BEFORE the haircut. The other two push integration cost out of year one, when it lands precisely at the moment of integration.

summary.keyIdea: A deal creates value when synergy discounted to today exceeds the premium paid - the rest is only scale
summary.commonMistake: Taking the synergy figure straight off the slide, ignoring integration costs, and assuming it all arrives in year one
summary.action: Haircut the synergy figure to between a half and seven tenths, deduct integration costs, then see whether the deal still stands

application.title: Try it on an announced deal
application.message: Find the premium over the price before the news broke, then find the synergy figure the buyer published. Discount the synergy to today and compare the two - most deals sit very close to the line.
application.secondary: If the buyer quotes synergy only at the full run rate without saying how long it takes to get there, that number is not yet comparable.

sections.text: Two kinds of synergy, and why the revenue half has to be discounted hard - that part was covered in the lesson on synergy in M&A. Here comes the next question: where the number on the slide comes from, why it is almost always optimistic, and how to cut it back to something usable.

Buyers typically pay 20-40% over the market price. That amount goes straight to the seller's shareholders, so the buyer has only synergy left to make it back. The compact rule: the present value of the synergy must exceed the premium, or the deal simply transfers value from the buyer's shareholders to the seller's. That is the right way to read the much-quoted finding that most mergers disappoint - they do not collapse, they overpay.
Three reasons the number is always optimistic

items: Whoever builds the number has an incentive for the deal to happen: the adviser earns a fee, management gets a bigger business to run
Synergy is hard to compute precisely, and anything hard to compute tends to get rounded upward
Integration always takes longer than planned - culture differences, IT systems to merge, and customers who may leave in the meantime

sections.text: Five ways to cut the optimism out

items: Haircut the number you were given to between a half and seven tenths before using it
Separate cost savings from revenue gains, and weight the cost half more heavily - it sits in the buyer's hands, the revenue half sits with the customers
Build a curve over time: synergy does not arrive in full in year one, it usually takes two to three years
Add the one-off integration cost into the model - it typically equals one to two years of synergy and is routinely left out
Run the sensitivity: if synergy reaches only seven tenths of plan, does the deal still stand up

sections.label: The full run rate is not year one
sections.text: Synergy figures are usually announced at the full run rate - the level reached once everything has settled. If the announcement does not say how long it takes to get there, that number cannot yet be compared with the premium, because the premium is paid today while the synergy arrives later.

lines: Deals rarely fail because the wrong target was picked; they fail because the right price was paid for a synergy that never showed up.
So the most arguable part of the model is not the multiple - it is the synergy number and the date it lands.
